source.title: DiffInf: Influence-Guided Diffusion for Supervision Alignment in Facial Attribute Learning
source.authors: Basudha Pal; Zhao-Yang Wang; Rama Chellappa

record.file_problem: Text appears to contain the full paper, including results and conclusion.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training and test performance under synthetic label noise and evaluates influence-guided sample correction, but it does not test the claim versions about random-label memorization, width, architecture comparisons, optimizer generalization, batch size, dropout, sharpness, or removing memorized examples as defined.
record.gate_note: The results concern robustness to deliberately injected label noise and the authors' data-repair method. They do not measure the listed claim versions. The paper's influence-ranking results are relevant background but do not test whether a measured network property tracks the natural-label train–test gap as V7 specifies.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates repair and removal of synthetically mislabeled facial images, not any supplied claim version. Its self-influence score is accumulated gradient energy, not V8's inclusion-based memorization measure or V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. It reports neither random-removal controls for V8 nor random-label fitting and matched natural-label performance for V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that repairing high-self-influence image–label mismatches improves facial attribute classification while retaining samples, outperforming removal in the main experiments and at 10–30% noise. The ablation qualifies this conclusion: removal performs better at 40% noise. Preservation of distributional coverage is an author interpretation supported by unchanged dataset size, rather than a directly measured coverage result.
record.recipe_differences: Trains a ResNet-18 with Adam on synthetic noisy facial labels, then uses influence-guided diffusion correction and retraining; it does not use the original studies' interventions or measures for the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level changes the relative outcome: generative correction outperforms removal at 10–30% noise, while removal slightly outperforms it at 40%.

fits_no_version.finding: On FFHQ, generative repair improves clean-test accuracy over noisy training and self-influence removal: age 83.37% versus 70.44% and 81.23%; expression 94.24% versus 78.95% and 93.42%. In the noise sweep, repair beats removal at 10–30% corruption but loses at 40%: 75.44% versus 77.14%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence-guided image repair can improve facial attribute classification under synthetic label noise, with its advantage over filtering depending on corruption severity.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 2 and 5 report higher checkpoint-based self-influence for corrupted samples and their concentration near the top of the ranking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Accumulated per-example gradient energy can help identify synthetic label corruption in facial attribute training.

record.problems: The paper studies only synthetic symmetric label noise in facial age and expression classification on FFHQ. It does not report uncertainty estimates for the stated performance metrics. The authors note interacting correction hyperparameters, approximate influence estimates, and that subgroup effects need further study.
record.rows_left_out: No rows qualify for the supplied claim versions. The paper's performance tables evaluate a different intervention and construct: repairing synthetic label-noise examples rather than the claim's specified memorization, generalization-gap, or network-property tests.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label training fit alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout effects, including dependence on dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking train–test gaps relative to competing measures.
Removal of examples ranked by inclusion-based memorization versus equally sized random removal, followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No qualifying rows or verdicts are needed. Improved accuracy after removing high-gradient noisy examples does not challenge V8 because neither its memorization criterion nor its random-removal comparison is measured.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected training and local connectivity comparisons.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization comparisons under different tuning regimes.
Large versus small batch effects and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train–test generalization gap.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples versus random-example removal.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
